title: Check yourself: balancing DRY with SRP

questions.stem: A shipping service had two methods with the same body, `String.format("%.1f kg", grams / 1000.0)`. One prints the weight on carrier labels, in a format the carrier specifies; the other shows it on the customer's order page. They were merged into `Units.kg(grams)`. Product now wants the order page to show two decimals, and the developer changes `Units.kg`. What happens to the labels?

options.text: They print two decimals as well, since two methods with one body were always one rule and change together
options.says: the same text can encode two rules; the carrier's format doesn't follow the order page, and only the shared body ties them

options.text: They print two decimals as well, since the label printer runs the one body the developer changed for the page
options.says: merging look-alike code ties two owners' rules together, so a change made for one reaches the other

options.text: They keep one decimal, since the label printer calls `Units.kg` with its own weights and the change was made for the page
options.says: both callers run the same body, so a change to it reaches every caller whatever arguments it passes

options.text: They keep one decimal, since only the order page's tests were changed along with the page's request
options.says: tests don't decide what shared code does; the label tests fail only if they hold the case

origin.section: Merging Look-Alike Code Ties Two Formats Together, and a Change for One Breaks the Other

questions.stem: `Report.render(rows, boolean html, boolean totals)` is called by the admin dashboard with `(rows, true, true)` and by the finance export, a plain-text file, with `(rows, false, true)`. The dashboard team asks for the totals row in bold, and the developer wraps it in `<b>` inside the `if (totals)` branch. Whose output changes?

options.text: Only the dashboard's, since the markup sits in the `totals` branch the dashboard asked to change
options.says: the finance export turns the same branch on, so it runs the new line too

options.text: Only the dashboard's, since the `html` flag keeps markup out of the finance export
options.says: a flag only separates callers where the body checks it; the new line sits in a branch that doesn't

options.text: Both, since the `totals` branch runs for each caller that passes `true` for it, `html` or not
options.says: the change went into a branch both callers reach, and nothing in it reads the `html` flag

options.text: Both, since `render` hands a change to every caller once the dashboard's own tests pass
options.says: tests don't route a change; it reaches the callers whose arguments take the branch it sits in

origin.section: A Flag for Each Caller Keeps the Method Shared, and Every Change Must Be Checked Against Both

questions.stem: `Notify.send(user, text, boolean sms, boolean urgent)` has two callers: the password reset passes `(true, true)` and the weekly digest passes `(false, false)`; with `sms` false the method sends email. You inline the method back into both callers. What does the digest's copy contain once you are done?

options.text: The whole body, with `sms` and `urgent` turned into local constants, since inlining moves the method into the caller as it is
options.says: copying the body is the first step; substituting the caller's values leaves branches that can't run, and they are deleted

options.text: The whole body, with `sms` and `urgent` kept as parameters, since a later digest request might need those branches
options.says: keeping another caller's branches keeps that caller's rules in the digest's code

options.text: The email path without the urgent handling, since the digest's own values leave the other branches unreachable
options.says: inlining copies the body, replaces each parameter with the caller's value, and deletes what can no longer run

options.text: The lines both callers ran, since the parts the two callers had in common are what inlining keeps
options.says: inlining keeps what this caller runs, not what the callers share

origin.section: Inlining the Method Back Gives Each Format Its Own Code, and All Checks Pass

questions.stem: A team finds the voucher rule "a code is valid until its expiry date and once per customer" written out in the checkout service and again in the mobile API, and nowhere else. What do they do?

options.text: Leave both copies until a third one appears, since two copies can't yet show which parts of the rule will vary
options.says: the rule of three is for when you can't tell; here the copies must change together, so they get one home now

options.text: Leave both copies in place, since each channel owns the voucher rule as it applies to that channel
options.says: the voucher rule is one rule with one owner; the next fix would reach one copy only

options.text: Move the rule into one place now, since any logic that appears twice should be extracted
options.says: look-alike code for different rules stays apart at any count; what decides is whether the copies must change together

options.text: Move the rule into one place now, since both copies must change whenever the voucher rule does
options.says: one rule gets one home at the second copy; the count matters only when you can't yet tell

origin.section: The Rule of Three Is a Heuristic for When You Can't Yet Tell
